summary: Ni-free duplex lightweight steel Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C (wt.%) after induction-furnace melting, solution treatment at 1250 °C for 35 min (argon) + water quenching, and isothermal annealing at 700 °C (one of the four annealing conditions 500/700/900/1050 °C). The 700 °C condition is the Ni-free counterpart used to establish how ordered precipitates — nano-sized cuboid κ-carbide in γ, needle-like κ in α and coarse FeAl-type B2 particles — control the local hardness; because the nano-scale cuboid κ cannot be probed directly by nano-indentation, its elastic constants were obtained by DFT.
composition: Nominal composition Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C (all in wt.%), i.e. a Ni-free duplex low-density (lightweight) steel: Fe base, 15 wt.% Mn, 10 wt.% Al and 0.8 wt.% C. It is the Ni-free member of a pair of alloys designed to compare the ordered NiAl- and FeAl-type B2 compounds and the κ-phase (L1′2) that form in both grades; the Al addition lowers mass density and, together with C and Mn, drives the precipitation of ordered κ-carbide and B2, while Mn substitution within κ governs its bonding and elastic response. The two alloys were selected specifically so that the nanomechanical properties of the ordered NiAl-type vs FeAl-type B2 and of κ could be separated. (In the paper's Tables 1 and 2 the same alloy is labelled Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.5C.)
processing: Processing lineage of this sample, in order: (1) the experimental alloys Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C-5Ni and Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C were melted in an induction furnace; (2) solution heat treatment for 35 min at 1250 °C in a protective argon atmosphere followed by water quenching — this is the parent process (proc_solution-treated-1250c-35min-wq) of the 700 °C anneal; (3) the material was cut into 3 mm (length) × 3 mm (width) × 1 mm (thickness) specimens; (4) isothermal annealing at 700 °C, one of four annealing treatments (500, 700, 900 and 1050 °C). The isothermal holding time at 700 °C is not explicitly reported in the paper; atmosphere and cooling medium for the annealing step are also not stated. The annealing temperature range was chosen to follow the sequence of ordered-phase formation (B2 at 900–1050 °C, κ-carbide at 500–700 °C).
microstructure: After the 700 °C anneal the Ni-free alloy shows a duplex γ (austenite, fcc) + α (ferrite, bcc) microstructure, and it remains γ + α at all four annealing temperatures (unlike the 5Ni alloy, whose matrix is γ alone at 500–700 °C). The γ grains are the darker equiaxed constituent and α forms bands. Nano-sized cuboid κ-carbide blocks (< 100 nm, Fe3AlC-type L1′2, ordered fcc/perovskite) precipitate inside the γ matrix, while needle-like κ-carbide (width 500 ± 33 nm at 700 °C, versus 200 ± 33 nm at 500 °C) forms within the α phase. Coarse FeAl-type B2 particles (2–4 μm, ordered bcc) are always present in the matrix (in γ, with grain-boundary B2 precipitates), but the α phase is NOT replaced by B2 stringer bands in this Ni-free grade — α + needle-like κ-carbide is retained instead, which is the key microstructural difference from the Ni-containing steel annealed at the same temperature. Four phases are therefore counted: γ, α, κ-carbide and coarse B2. Grain size, texture and volume fractions are not reported.
properties: Nano-indentation (constant loading/unloading rate 500 μN s⁻¹ to a maximum load of 10000 μN, hold time 20 s, each measurement repeated at least 25 times in arrays of 50–70 indents; compound hardness of matrix plus particles on 3 × 3 × 1 mm specimens) gives for this Ni-free alloy at 700 °C: γ + cuboid κ = 7 GPa and α + needle-like κ = 6.7 GPa. For reference, the solution-treated single phases measured 4 GPa (γ) and 3 GPa (α). The needle-like κ-carbide formed in α at 700 °C contains a higher Mn content (≈24.8 wt.%) than that formed at 500 °C (≈18.4 wt.%), parallel to the higher α + κ hardness (6.7 vs 5.3 GPa). No tensile, fracture, fatigue, creep, physical, chemical or radiation data are reported for this sample. Characterization techniques applied: Field Emission SEM (Carl Zeiss Sigma, 20 kV, with high-speed X-ray EDS, specimens polished and etched in 5% nital), TEM (JEOL 2000FX; bright-field imaging and selected-area diffraction patterns; thin foils twin-jet electro-polished in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 25 V), and instrumented nano-indentation. Supporting DFT (Quantum-ESPRESSO, spin-polarized GGA-PBE, ultrasoft pseudopotentials) supplied the elastic constants, bulk/shear/Young's moduli and anisotropy factor of Fe3AlC, Fe2MnAlC, FeMn2AlC and Mn3AlC κ-carbides.
mechanisms: Annealing temperature → κ composition and size: raising the isothermal temperature from 500 to 700 °C coarsens the needle-like κ in α (width 200 ± 33 nm → 500 ± 33 nm) and enriches it in Mn (≈18.4 → ≈24.8 wt.%), which changes the formation energy, lattice parameter and magnetization of the κ-phase and yields harder κ particles; this is reflected in the α + κ composite hardness rising from 5.3 GPa (500 °C) to 6.7 GPa (700 °C).

Composition (Ni-free) → phase selection in α: without Ni, the α phase is not consumed into B2 stringer bands at 500–700 °C; instead needle-like κ-carbide precipitates within α (α + κ), whereas in the 5Ni steel the whole α phase converts to B2 stringer bands; because κ is intrinsically less shear-resistant than B2, the Ni-free α + κ composite (6.7 GPa at 700 °C) is far softer than the Ni-containing B2 stringer band (10.6 GPa at 700 °C).

Precipitate size → hardness (Orowan-type strengthening): the increase in shear stress scales as Δτ ∝ R^−1.25, so smaller, finely and uniformly dispersed nano-scale precipitates raise the resistance to shear; this explains why composite structures containing ordered precipitates (γ + κ, α + κ, γ + B2, α + B2) are markedly harder (≈6–10 GPa) than the parent single-phase γ and α (~3–4 GPa) in both alloys.

Bond chemistry in κ → elastic stiffness: substituting Fe by Mn in the κ structure replaces weaker Fe–C bonds with stronger Mn–C bonds, increasing the bulk modulus, shear modulus and Young's modulus of the κ-phase; the DFT elastic constants of Mn3AlC exceed those of Fe3AlC, directly rationalizing the experimentally observed hardening of Mn-enriched κ formed at 700 °C relative to 500 °C.

C insertion → κ stiffening: occupation of the octahedral interstitial site of the L1′2 structure by C rigidifies Fe3AlC relative to Fe3Al through strong Fe–C bonds along <100> directions (C11 of Fe3AlC(sp) = 450 GPa vs 181 GPa for Fe3Al), i.e. the interstitial C is what makes the κ-phase a stiff, weakly shearable precipitate.

Elastic anisotropy of κ: the calculated anisotropy factor of κ is greater than 1 (Cα = 2.39 from the acoustic method, 2.47 from the lattice-distortion method), so E111 < E100 for the κ-phase; the simultaneously high shear modulus of Fe3AlC explains the experimentally observed un-shearable nature of these precipitates.

Ni addition → B2 bond strength (comparison): Ni–Al bonds are stronger than Fe–Al bonds (higher elastic constants and more negative enthalpy of formation for B2-(Fe,Ni)-Al than B2-Fe-Al), so replacing FeAl-type B2 by NiAl-type B2 in the Ni-containing steel raises the peak hardness from 7.2 GPa to 9 GPa; the absence of Ni is one reason the Ni-free alloy annealed at 700 °C reaches only ≈7 GPa in γ + κ and 6.7 GPa in α + κ.

Lattice expansion from Mn: Mn has a larger atomic radius (rMn = 1.61 Å) than Fe (rFe = 1.56 Å), so progressive Mn substitution expands the κ lattice parameter from 3.78 Å (Fe2MnAlC) to 3.84 Å (Mn3AlC), consistent with the calculated elastic-constant increase in Mn-rich κ.
conclusions: For the Ni-free Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C steel annealed at 700 °C, nano-indentation gives a compound hardness of 7 GPa for γ + cuboid κ-carbide and 6.7 GPa for α + needle-like κ-carbide, against 4 GPa (γ) and 3 GPa (α) in the solution-treated state. The 700 °C condition is where the two alloys diverge most clearly: in the Ni-free grade α retains needle-like κ (width 500 ± 33 nm, ≈24.8 wt.% Mn) instead of transforming to B2 stringer bands, so its hardness stays below the Ni-containing counterparts annealed at the same temperature (B2 stringer 10.6 GPa; γ + κ + B2 9 GPa). Overall the addition of Ni raises peak hardness from 7.2 GPa to 9 GPa in both austenite and ferrite, attributed to Ni–Al bonds replacing Fe–Al bonds in the B2 phase. Because isolated nano-sized cuboid κ particles cannot be measured by nano-indentation, their elastic constants were supplied by first-principles DFT, which confirmed that C insertion and especially Mn substitution stiffen the κ-phase; this links precipitate chemistry directly to bulk hardness and provides a basis for designing low-density Fe-Mn-Al-C steels with tailored ordered precipitates.
unmapped: Nomenclature discrepancy: the paper's main text and Methods call the Ni-free grade Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C (wt.%), while Tables 1 and 2 (and the sample alias list) render it as Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.5C.
The isothermal holding time for the 700 °C anneal is not reported, nor are the annealing atmosphere and cooling medium after annealing.

Nano-indentation in this study measures a compound hardness of nano/micro features embedded in their surrounding matrix and cannot isolate single nano-sized particles; consequently the hardness of the nano-sized cuboid κ in γ (and of isolated nano-disc B2) was not measured directly but estimated via DFT. Changing indenter size or load would introduce a nano-indentation size effect that could obscure the real influence of precipitate size on composite hardness.

The SEM micrographs presented (Fig. 2) show the Ni-containing sample; the Ni-free alloy is stated to follow a similar trend except that α + needle-like κ-carbides occur at 500–700 °C instead of B2 stringer bands, so the direct micrographs for this sample's own microstructure are limited.
Coarse FeAl-type B2 particles (2–4 μm) are reported as always present in the Ni-free alloy at all four annealing temperatures, but no volume fraction or grain size is given.

Elemental contents of the B2 particles (≈18.3–19.1 wt.% Al) and of the nano-disc B2 in α (≈22.9–24.7 wt.% Al) are reported only for the 900 and 1050 °C conditions and are therefore not part of the 700 °C state of this sample.
